name: 1-Androsterone (1-Andro)

lead: 1-Androsterone (1-Andro, 1-DHEA) is an oral designer steroid sold online as a dietary supplement for muscle gain. Chemically it is an isomer of DHEA.

It is described as a prohormone converted in the body to 1-testosterone and related androgens, which act on the androgen receptor. It appears in the literature mainly through a 2011 study of a product seized by German investigators, which characterised its urinary elimination for doping control. No human trials of its effects were found.

paras: It has been sold as an oral supplement, usually in capsule products marketed to lifters. No documented routine or timeline exists.
No human safety data exist. Authorities and anti-doping bodies treat such designer androgens as pharmacologically related to anabolic steroids.

angle.text: 1-Andro is sold as a prohormone that converts to 1-testosterone and related androgens, for more muscle mass. It is known from seizure and doping-detection papers, and no human trials exist.

lead: 1-Androsterone, sold as 1-Andro or 1-DHEA, is a synthetic oral androgen that has been marketed online as a "dietary supplement" for building muscle. Chemically it is 3β-hydroxy-5α-androst-1-en-17-one, a positional isomer of the hormone DHEA [1][2]. Buyers are after the physique payoff of androgens: more lean mass, fuller shoulders and chest, and a more muscular frame.

It is described as a prohormone, meaning a compound that the body is said to convert into an active hormone, in this case 1-testosterone (dihydroboldenone) and related 1-dehydrogenated androstanes, which act on the androgen receptor [1]. A closely related product, 1-androstenediol, is also described as a prohormone of 1-testosterone that has been sold as a supplement and appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of prohibited substances [3].

The compound is documented mainly in analytical chemistry. A 2011 study identified it in a product seized by German criminal investigators and characterised its urinary elimination so that anti-doping laboratories could detect it [2]. A 2019 paper described a way to measure designer steroids in supplements when reference standards are unavailable [4]. No human efficacy or safety trials were found.

paras: Wikipedia lists 1-androsterone under several names, including 1-Andro, 1-DHEA, 1-prasterone and 5α-androst-1-en-3β-ol-17-one, with formula C19H28O2, molar mass about 288.4 g/mol and CAS number 23633-63-8. It is a positional isomer of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), differing in where the double bond sits in the steroid skeleton, and is described as synthetic and orally active. The Wikipedia entry is marked as a stub [1].

The 2011 identification study describes the compound as 3β-hydroxy-5α-androst-1-en-17-one, found in a product from a brand sold as a supplement and seized by criminal investigators in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany [2].

The supplement category that 1-Andro belongs to grew out of US regulation. The Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 1990 placed anabolic steroids in Schedule III and defined them as drugs or hormonal substances chemically and pharmacologically related to testosterone [5]. The 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act allowed products to be sold as supplements without pre-market approval [6], and in the following years companies sold prohormones, compounds expected to convert in the body into steroids, as muscle supplements [2][7].

Legislation later widened the definitions: an Anabolic Steroid Control Act in 2004 redefined anabolic steroids and listed specific substances, and the Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2014 added about two dozen more and set penalties for mislabelled products [5][8]. 1-Androsterone, identified in a product seized by German investigators in 2011, was characterised in analytical chemistry literature as new analogues that had not been approved as drugs [2].

Wikipedia describes 1-androsterone as a prohormone that converts to 1-testosterone, 1-androstenedione and other 1-dehydrogenated androstanes, and lists it among androgen receptor agonists [1]. The published literature gives no pharmacokinetic data beyond the urinary elimination work in the 2011 identification study [2].

Wikipedia classifies it among androgen receptor modulators derived from 5α-dihydrotestosterone and describes it as a prohormone of 1-testosterone (dihydroboldenone) and 1-androstenedione [1]. A T Nation moderator comment says it relies on enzymatic conversions and is not itself directly active, in contrast to the compound 11-T [9].

The authors of the 2011 identification study note that new androgen analogues never approved as drugs are marketed as supplements, mainly advertised for muscle mass, and that government authorities and WADA regard them as pharmacologically or chemically related to anabolic steroids [2]. Analytical chemists have also published methods for quantifying emerging designer steroids in supplements where reference materials are scarce [4].

In the United States, dietary supplements are sold under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, which does not require government approval before sale. A 2007 to 2016 analysis cited by Wikipedia found 776 supplements with unlisted pharmaceutical ingredients, and reported that muscle-building supplements were contaminated with anabolic steroids [6].

The 2014 Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act, signed in the United States on 18 December 2014, expanded the list of regulated anabolic steroids by about two dozen substances and allowed the Attorney General to add substances by temporary order; it also introduced penalties for mislabelled steroid products [8]. The act's text does not name 1-androsterone, according to Wikipedia's summary of it [8].

On T Nation, the older 'ProHormones - All You Need to Know' thread (2008) includes users asking whether androsterone-type products are safer than other prohormones and replies that they are banned or that other compounds are preferable [7]. Another thread of the same period distinguishes 1-androsterone from 11-T by noting that the former needs conversion [9]. Forum material of this kind is mostly historical, from an era when prohormone supplements were sold openly.

The Anabolic Steroid Control Act's background includes the mid-1980s removal of anabolic steroids from the pharmaceutical market by an FDA review, a period in which an illicit market grew, according to Wikipedia [5].

No studies found. The published literature consists of analytical studies on identification and urinary detection [2][4]. Research on the related endogenous steroid androsterone examines its metabolism in human lung tissue [10] and its effects on plants [11], which concern the natural compound rather than this designer isomer.
